_notes: E1 R1.7 — the Holy See's diplomatic service (docs/EXPANSION-E1-ROME.md §11.4). Scenes of the Academy and the nunciature are drawn from the ordinary pool of a man away (requiring the posting's flag and, for some, his rank or his post's hardship); the missionary year, the rotation, the nuncio's terna, and the letter at seventy-five are the service's own beat, fired when due. Effects move the posting's dials and book through `place` and `record`; `diplomat:go_home` asks to be released at a rotation. Every person is generated; the countries are real and the Church there is summarized, flagged.

events.title: The First Dinner
events.body: The Academy's first dinner of the year: thirty-odd priests from twenty countries at one long table, the president at the head, and a place card that puts you between a Nigerian who has a doctorate in international law and a Pole who has already been told he is going to Moscow. The president asks each man, in turn, what language he dreams in.

choices.label: Say English, and that you hope to dream in others
choices.outcome: You say English, and that you hope to add to it. The Nigerian laughs and says he dreams in four and argues in five. By dessert the three of you have a table of your own for the year.

choices.label: Say Latin, which gets a laugh
choices.outcome: You say Latin. It gets the laugh you wanted and a look from the president you did not; he has heard it every year for twenty years. It is still a good dinner.

events.title: The Language That Will Not Come
events.body: Four months of French and it will not come: you read it well enough and cannot say a sentence without building it first, like furniture. The teacher, a nun from Lyon with no patience for men who translate in their heads, has given you a choice she clearly thinks is no choice at all.

choices.label: Spend the summer in a French parish, and speak nothing else
choices.outcome: You spend the summer in a parish in the Auvergne, where the pastor is eighty and speaks no English on principle. By August you are dreaming in it, badly. The nun says nothing when you come back, which from her is a medal.

choices.label: Grind it out at the desk, a grammar and a notebook
choices.outcome: You grind it out at the desk. It comes, slowly, the way cement sets. You will always speak it like a man reading a contract, and the service is full of such men.

events.title: The Professor Who Was a Nuncio
events.body: The lecturer on diplomatic practice is a retired nuncio, eighty-one, who was expelled from one country and shot at in another. After class he keeps you back and asks what you think the service is for. He does not accept the first answer, or the second.

choices.label: Say: to protect the local Church
choices.outcome: You say it is to protect the local Church when nobody else will. He nods slowly and says that is the right answer, and that the Secretariat will sometimes ask you to forget it, and that you must not.

choices.label: Say: to keep a door open between Rome and every government
choices.outcome: You say the service keeps a door open between Rome and governments that have closed every other. He says that is the answer that gets men made nuncio, and that it is also true, and that he is not sure which of those he meant as a compliment.

events.title: Where Would You Like to Go
events.body: A counsellor from the Secretariat's personnel office comes to lunch at the Academy and asks each man, over coffee, where he would like to be sent. Everyone at the table knows the answer changes nothing; the Secretariat sends men where it needs them, and the needs are decided in rooms none of you has seen. Everyone also knows it is written down.

choices.label: Say you will go anywhere, and mean somewhere hard
choices.outcome: You say anywhere, and that you would rather be useful than comfortable. He writes something down. The man next to you, who said Vienna, is sent to Vienna in the end, and you are not.

choices.label: Say somewhere with a language you have
choices.outcome: You say somewhere with a language you already have, where you could be of use from the first day. He writes that down too, and says that is the most sensible answer he has heard this year, which is not the same as a promise.

events.title: A Letter from Your Bishop
events.body: {@bishop} writes from home: two pastors have died this year and one has left, the diocese is short in a way it has not been before, and he wonders, without asking, whether the Academy is really where you are needed. He would not stand in your way. He would like you to know the parishes miss you.

choices.label: Write back that you will stay the course
choices.outcome: You write back that you will stay the course, and that you are sorry, and that you pray for the diocese every day, which is true. His reply is a line: he understands, and he will not ask again. He does not.

choices.label: Tell him you will ask the Academy whether you might go home
choices.outcome: You tell him you will ask. The president of the Academy listens, and says that a man who is asking already has one foot in the parish, and that the Church needs pastors more than it needs secretaries of nunciature. He lets you finish the year. You do not go home, in the end; but you are not sure, for a year, that you were right.

events.title: The Missionary Year
events.body: The missionary year: the Academy sends its men for twelve months to a local Church somewhere poor. Yours is a diocese of the interior reached by a road that washes out in the rains, a bishop with forty priests for three hundred thousand Catholics, and a parish of nine villages whose pastor has malaria and has been waiting for help since before you were ordained.

choices.label: Take the villages: a motorbike, a Mass kit, and nine Sundays a month
choices.outcome: You take the villages. You learn to ride the motorbike, and to say Mass under a tree, and to hear confessions through an interpreter who is also the catechist and also somebody's grandmother. You come back to Rome thinner and with a different idea of what a nuncio is for.

choices.label: Help the bishop in his chancery: his files are years behind
choices.outcome: You help the bishop with his chancery, which is two rooms and a typewriter and ten years of Rome's letters unanswered. You answer them. He tells the nuncio, who tells the Secretariat, that the Academy sent him a man who can work.

events.title: The Nuncio's Temper
events.body: {@nuncio_chief} is a good diplomat and a hard man to work for: he rewrites every dispatch, calls you at eleven at night about a comma, and tonight has sent back your report on the elections with a single word written across it in red ink. The word is: no.

choices.label: Knock on his door and ask what he meant
choices.outcome: You knock on his door. He is in a cardigan with a glass of grappa, and he talks for an hour about the country, and it turns out he meant that the report was right and too early. You rewrite it. He signs it. You are, after that, the man he calls at eleven for something other than commas.

choices.label: Redraft it without asking, and again, until he signs
choices.outcome: You redraft it without asking, four times, each version saying a little less, until he signs. It goes to Rome. Rome does not notice. He does, and does not quite respect it.

events.title: The Night of the Coup
events.body: At two in the morning there is shooting near the presidential palace, and by four the radio is playing martial music. The nuncio is in Rome on leave. At six a minister of the fallen government and his family are at the nunciature's gate, asking to come in. The Vienna Convention says the nunciature is inviolable. The soldiers across the road have not read it.

choices.label: Open the gate
choices.outcome: You open the gate. The minister, his wife, and three children sleep in the nunciature's guest rooms for eleven weeks, while you telephone Rome twice a day and the soldiers across the road watch you walk to the chapel. In the end they leave for the airport in the nunciature's car with its flag, and you ride in the front seat.

choices.label: Telephone Rome first, and keep them at the gate until it answers
choices.outcome: You telephone Rome. Rome takes three hours to call back, which is fast for Rome, and says to let them in. In the three hours, the soldiers take the minister's eldest son away for questioning. He comes back a week later. You are not sure you will ever forgive yourself the three hours.

events.title: A Letter Behind the Nuncio's Back
events.body: A bishop of the country asks to see you alone after a Mass. He gives you a sealed letter addressed to the Prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops and asks you to send it in the diplomatic bag without the nuncio's knowledge: it is about the nuncio's candidate for the country's largest see, and it is not kind.

choices.label: Tell him you cannot, and that he must give it to the nuncio himself
choices.outcome: You tell him you cannot carry a letter your chief does not know about, and that he must give it to the nuncio himself, sealed, which the nuncio is bound to send. He does. The nuncio sends it, and says nothing to you, and the candidate is not named.

choices.label: Carry it: a bishop has a right to write to Rome
choices.outcome: You carry it. A bishop has a right to write to Rome, and you tell yourself that is all you are doing. The nuncio finds out in a month, as nuncios do, and the temperature in the nunciature drops for a year.

events.title: A Report Softened
events.body: Your report on the government's treatment of a religious minority is accurate and damning. {@nuncio_chief} reads it, agrees with every word, and asks you to soften it: the Secretariat is negotiating an agreement with this government, and a report that reaches the wrong desk in Rome could end the negotiation and, with it, the schools the agreement would protect.

choices.label: Soften it: the schools are real too
choices.outcome: You soften it. The agreement is signed the next year, and the schools are protected, and the minority is not, quite. You keep a copy of the first draft in your own files, dated, in case anyone ever asks what the nunciature knew.

choices.label: Send it as written, with a covering note from you
choices.outcome: You send it as written, with a covering note saying the nuncio's view differs, which he permits with a face you will not forget. The negotiation stalls for a year. A counsellor in Rome writes to you, privately, that your report was the only honest thing he read that month.

events.title: The Journalist
events.body: A foreign correspondent you have met at three receptions asks you to lunch and, over the second course, asks for the nunciature's view of the bishops' statement on the election. Not for attribution. She is good, she is fair, and she will print whatever you say in some form.

choices.label: Say nothing, pleasantly, for an hour
choices.outcome: You say nothing, pleasantly, for an hour, and pay for lunch. She writes her piece without you, and it is fair. She asks you to lunch again, which in her trade is respect.

choices.label: Give her a little background, on deep background
choices.outcome: You give her a little, on deep background, carefully. It appears as 'a diplomat familiar with the Church's thinking', and the nuncio reads it at breakfast and knows exactly which diplomat.

events.title: The Pope's Day
events.body: The anniversary of the pope's election is the Holy See's national day: a reception at the nunciature for the diplomatic corps, the government, the bishops, and whoever the cook has decided to feed. You are responsible for the guest list, and the foreign minister's office has asked, delicately, that a certain opposition leader not be invited.

choices.label: Invite him: the nunciature invites whom it invites
choices.outcome: You invite him. The foreign minister sends his deputy instead of coming himself, which is a message, and the opposition leader stands in the garden for two hours talking to bishops, which is another. The nuncio says, afterwards, that it was a good reception.

choices.label: Leave him off, and send him a note
choices.outcome: You leave him off the list and send him a handwritten note regretting that the garden is small. The foreign minister comes in person. The opposition leader keeps the note, and shows it to people.

events.title: A Priest Who Needs Protecting
events.body: A priest of the country, who preached last month about the disappearances in the north, comes to the nunciature at night. He has been followed for a week. His bishop has told him to be quiet. He asks whether the Holy See can do anything for a priest who will not be quiet.

choices.label: Make him visible: invite him to the nunciature's Mass, publicly, every week
choices.outcome: You invite him to concelebrate at the nunciature's Sunday Mass, every week, where the diplomatic corps and the government's observers can see him standing beside the pope's representative. He is followed for another year. He is not arrested.

choices.label: Report it to Rome and advise him to leave the country for a time
choices.outcome: You report it to Rome and help him to a scholarship abroad, for a year, which becomes three. He is safe. His parish is given to a man who is quiet, and the disappearances in the north are not preached about again.

events.title: A Letter from Home
events.body: A letter from home in your sister's hand: your mother fell in the spring, and is better, and is asking, the way she asks, when you are coming home for more than a week. The Secretariat gives a man a month a year. You have not taken yours in two.

choices.label: Take the month, and go home
choices.outcome: You take the month and go home. Your mother is smaller than you remember, and sharper, and she asks you whether the pope is well as if you had lunch with him yesterday. You say Mass at the kitchen table on the last morning.

choices.label: Write that you will come at Christmas
choices.outcome: You write that you will come at Christmas, and there is a crisis at Christmas, as there always is. You come at Easter. She is fine, and she tells you, twice, that she was fine at Christmas too.

events.title: Chargé d'Affaires
events.body: The nuncio is in hospital in Rome for six weeks, and you are chargé d'affaires ad interim: the nunciature is yours. The government chooses this week to announce a law that will take the Church's schools into state control from the new year, and the bishops want to know what the Holy See is going to do.

choices.label: Stand with the bishops publicly, and let Rome catch up
choices.outcome: You stand with the bishops publicly: a statement from the nunciature, read at the conference, that the Holy See regards the law as a breach of the agreement. Rome is startled, and then, when the government withdraws the law in a month, pleased. The nuncio, back from hospital, is pleased in a way that has an edge.

choices.label: Work the ministries quietly, and keep Rome informed hourly
choices.outcome: You work the ministries quietly, three meetings a day, and send Rome a cable every evening. The law is delayed, amended, delayed again. It is never withdrawn and never enforced. That is how most of these things end.

events.title: Credentials
events.body: You present your letters of credence to the head of state in {country}: a band, an honour guard, a room with a portrait of the man in front of you, and ten minutes of conversation that both of you have prepared and neither of you will quote. At the end he asks, off the protocol, whether the pope really reads the reports.

choices.label: Say yes, and that he reads them closely
choices.outcome: You say yes, and that he reads them closely. It is true of some reports. The president looks at you for a moment longer than protocol allows, and you understand that you have just been told something about how he will treat the Church.

choices.label: Say the pope reads the letters of the Church in this country more closely still
choices.outcome: You say the pope reads the letters of the Church in this country even more closely than the reports. The president smiles, not warmly. The bishops hear about it by evening.

events.title: Preparing a Papal Visit
events.body: The Holy Father will visit {country} in eight months, and the nunciature is where the visit is made: the programme, the security, the Mass for half a million, the government's wish for a photograph at the palace, and the bishops' wish for a visit to a place the government would rather the world did not see.

choices.label: Put the place on the programme, and let the government argue with Rome
choices.outcome: You put it on the programme. The government argues for four months, with Rome and with you. The pope goes there, for forty minutes, and the photograph that goes round the world is not the one at the palace.

choices.label: Give the government its day, and the bishops a private meeting
choices.outcome: You give the government its day at the palace and the bishops a private hour with the pope, where they say everything they would have said in public. The visit is called a success by everyone, which is what visits are for.

events.title: The Bishops' Conference
events.body: The bishops' conference of {country} is split down the middle over a pastoral letter on the government, and both halves have come to the nunciature in the same week to ask the nuncio which side Rome is on. Rome, as far as you can tell from the cables, is on the side of the conference not splitting.

choices.label: Bring both halves to dinner at the nunciature and keep them there until they agree
choices.outcome: You have them all to dinner and keep them there until one in the morning. The letter that comes out is weaker than either half wanted and signed by all of them, which in a bishops' conference is a miracle of the second class.

choices.label: Refer it to Rome, and let the Dicastery settle it
choices.outcome: You refer it to Rome. The Dicastery takes six months and settles it by asking for no letter at all. Both halves blame the nuncio, which is what nuncios are for.

events.title: Persona Non Grata
events.body: The foreign ministry summons you on a Tuesday and hands you a note: the government regards the nuncio's statements on the treatment of priests in the north as interference in its internal affairs, and requests that he leave the country within seventy-two hours. The bishops are waiting outside the ministry to see what you will do.

choices.label: Leave with dignity, and say why at the airport
choices.outcome: You leave with dignity, and at the airport, in front of the cameras, you say that the Holy See's representative has been expelled for speaking about priests in prison. The Secretariat is not pleased by the airport. The bishops keep the recording.

choices.label: Leave quietly: a chargé stays, and the door must not close
choices.outcome: You leave quietly, and a chargé d'affaires stays behind, and the Holy See keeps a door open to a government that has closed every other. The priests in the north stay in prison, some of them, for a while.

events.title: The Other Side of the Terna
events.body: A see of {country} is vacant, and the consultation is done: forty letters out, sub secreto, and thirty-two back. Three names go to Rome in the bag. On your desk: a seminary rector everyone admires and nobody knows, a chancellor who has run the diocese for ten years under a sick bishop, and a pastor in the slums who is loved and has once been reported for saying what he thinks. Once, a nuncio's secretary called you about someone like each of them.

choices.label: Put the pastor first
choices.outcome: You put the pastor first, with a page explaining the report and why it should not count. Rome names him. At his ordination he preaches for eight minutes and says nothing a government could quote, which you did not expect, and then the next year he says it.

choices.label: Put the chancellor first
choices.outcome: You put the chancellor first: the diocese needs running, and he has been running it. Rome names him. The diocese is well run and nobody is surprised by anything, and a few of the young priests, you hear, have stopped hoping for much.

choices.label: Put the rector first
choices.outcome: You put the rector first: the priests trust him, and a bishop who has formed half his presbyterate starts with their trust. Rome names him. The seminary gets a new rector who is not as good, which is the price.

events.title: The Letter at Seventy-Five
events.body: On your seventy-fifth birthday you write the letter every nuncio writes: that you place your office in the Holy Father's hands. The Secretariat answers in a month, with thanks, and a date. {country} gives you a dinner. You have served as {diplomat_rank} and in every rank below it, and you find you do not know where to go now that no one is sending you.

choices.label: Go home, to the diocese that ordained you
choices.outcome: You go home to the diocese that ordained you, to a room in a retirement house for priests, where the other old men are pastors and cannot imagine what you did all those years, and you find that you do not mind.

choices.label: Stay in Rome, in a room near the Secretariat
choices.outcome: You stay in Rome, in a room in a house for retired diplomats of the Holy See, where the other old men were nuncios too, and the conversation at dinner is in six languages and mostly about who was wrong in 1989.

events.title: The Secretariat Has No Rung for You
events.body: The letter that should name your next country names none. It is signed by the assessor himself, which is the Secretariat's way of being kind. Ten years in the service, and the counsellors' list has not had your name on it: the reports were read, the nuncios were fond of you, and the men who go higher went past you in the corridor without malice. The service does not keep a secretary forever; it thanks him. You are thanked, in two sentences, and asked what you would like to do.

choices.label: Ask to be released to go home to your diocese
choices.outcome: You write the letter that afternoon, and it is easier than you expected. The Secretariat's answer is warm and three paragraphs long, which is two more than most men get. Your bishop writes that there is a parish, and that he had begun to wonder whether he would ever get you back.

choices.label: Ask for a desk at the Secretariat instead
choices.outcome: You write that you would rather not leave the Holy See's service altogether, and ask whether there is a desk. The answer takes a month and says that there may be, and that the Secretariat will write to your bishop. You go home to wait for a letter you half believe in, with ten years of other men's countries in your head.

choices.label: Ask for one more country, and then go
choices.outcome: You ask for one more country. The letter says yes, in the tone of a man granting a favour he has granted before and will not grant twice. You will go where they send you, for three years, and then you will go home, and both of you know it.

events.title: No Nunciature
events.body: The assessor telephones, which he does not do, and asks you to come to Rome for a day. In his office on the Third Loggia he says what the file has said for some years: there are more counsellors than nunciatures, the Holy Father has his own list, and your name, which has been on the Secretariat's, is not on his. He says it without unkindness; he has said it to better men. A counsellor who will not be a nuncio goes home, or to a desk in this building, and the Secretariat would like to know which.

choices.label: Ask to be released to go home to your diocese
choices.outcome: You write the letter that afternoon, and it is easier than you expected. The Secretariat's answer is warm and three paragraphs long, which is two more than most men get. Your bishop writes that there is a parish, and that he had begun to wonder whether he would ever get you back.

choices.label: Ask for a desk at the Secretariat instead
choices.outcome: You write that you would rather not leave the Holy See's service altogether, and ask whether there is a desk. The answer takes a month and says that there may be, and that the Secretariat will write to your bishop. You go home to wait for a letter you half believe in, with eighteen years of other men's countries in your head.

choices.label: Ask for one more country, and then go
choices.outcome: You ask for one more country. The letter says yes, in the tone of a man granting a favour he has granted before and will not grant twice. You will go where they send you, for three years, and then you will go home, and both of you know it.

events.title: Your First Dispatch
events.body: Your first dispatch to Rome comes back from {@nuncio_chief}'s desk with every paragraph struck through and one sentence of yours left standing, circled. He says it is a good sentence and the rest is a seminarian's essay, and that a dispatch is four pages the Secretary of State can read in a car. He wants it again by six.

choices.label: Write it again his way, four pages, by six
choices.outcome: You write it his way. It is better, and you resent that it is better, and by the third dispatch you cannot remember writing any other way. He initials it without reading it, which is the highest praise the house gives.

choices.label: Write it again, and keep three of your sentences
choices.outcome: You keep three sentences. He strikes two. The one that survives is quoted back to the nunciature in a letter from the Secretariat four months later, unsigned, in a paragraph that begins 'as the nunciature has observed'. You do not tell him it was yours. He knows.

events.title: The Cook
events.body: The nunciature's cook has outlasted four nuncios and intends to outlast {@nuncio_chief}. She tells you, in a kitchen you were not invited into, which minister's wife is Catholic, which bishop drinks, and why the last secretary left early. The nuncio eats in the dining room, alone, with a book. She has set a second place at the kitchen table and is waiting to see what kind of priest you are.

choices.label: Eat in the kitchen
choices.outcome: You eat in the kitchen, most nights, for three years. You learn the country from her before you learn it from anyone, and when the nuncio asks you how you knew about the minister's wife you say a parishioner told you, which is true.

choices.label: Eat with the nuncio, as the house expects
choices.outcome: You eat in the dining room, with the nuncio and his book, and learn the service from him instead. She feeds you anyway, and tells you less, and when you leave she says you were a good secretary, which from her is not a compliment.

events.title: The Language on the Street
events.body: The second country has a second language, and the nunciature's French and Italian do not reach the market. You can learn it from the embassy's tutor, in the mornings, at the Secretariat's expense, or from the parish down the road, on Sundays, from people who will laugh at you.

choices.label: The parish, on Sundays, and the market every morning
choices.outcome: You are laughed at for a year and understood in the second. The nuncio notices that the bishops talk to you in a language he does not have, and says nothing, and sends you to the ones he cannot read.

choices.label: The embassy's tutor, properly, in the mornings
choices.outcome: You learn it properly, with the grammar, from a woman who has taught four ambassadors. You can read the newspaper in six months and the ministry's letters in nine. The market still laughs at you, in a friendlier way.

events.title: The Fourth of July
events.body: The American embassy's invitation comes in a thick envelope: the Fourth of July reception, the ambassador's residence, the only American priest in the diplomatic corps requested. {@nuncio_chief} reads it and says that the Holy See has no country and that you are its man here, not Washington's, and then says that you should probably go, and that he will want to know who was there.

choices.label: Go, and remember who was there
choices.outcome: You go. The ambassador calls you Father and then, after the second drink, asks what the nuncio really thinks of the president. You tell him the nuncio thinks very highly of everyone, which is in the training. Your report on who was there runs to two pages and is the most useful thing you write that year.

choices.label: Send regrets, as the Holy See's man
choices.outcome: You send regrets on the nunciature's card. The ambassador's deputy telephones to ask whether anything is wrong, and you say nothing is wrong, and the Secretariat, which reads everything, notes that the nunciature's American is not at the Americans' table, and approves.

events.title: A New Nuncio
events.body: {@nuncio_chief} is seventy-five, and the letter has come for him as it comes for everyone. His successor arrives in a month, from a country you have never been to, with a reputation for reading every draft twice. The old man spends his last fortnight telling you what to keep from the new one and what to show him, and gives you his pen, which does not work.

choices.label: Learn the new man, and let the drafts be rewritten
choices.outcome: The new nuncio rewrites your first month's drafts entirely and your third month's hardly at all. You learn his sentences the way you learned the old man's. The pen sits in your drawer.

choices.label: Argue the paragraphs that matter
choices.outcome: You argue three paragraphs in the first month, and win one, and the new nuncio, who was told you were easy, revises his view. He tells Rome you have opinions. Rome, which likes to know that about a man early, writes it down.

events.title: A Letter from a Pastor
events.body: A letter from a classmate, in the hand you remember from the seminary's noticeboard: he has been made pastor of a parish with a school and a debt, and writes to say so, and to ask what it is like to have lunch with ambassadors. There is a photograph of him in a hard hat in front of the school's new roof. You have not had a parish, and may never have one.

choices.label: Write him the truth
choices.outcome: You write that it is like being a curate in a house with one priest and a flag, that you say Mass for the cook and a guard, and that you envy him the roof. He writes back that he envies you the ambassadors, and that the roof leaks. You keep the letter.

choices.label: Write him the postcard version
choices.outcome: You write about the ambassadors and the national day and the time the president's car came for you. It is all true. He reads it to the parish council, who are impressed, and you do not hear from him for four years.

events.title: The Bishop Wants You Home
events.body: {@bishop} writes, not through the Secretariat but to you, which bishops are not supposed to do and all of them do. He is short of men who can read a budget and a room, the chancery needs a vicar for something, and he has watched your name go round the world for six years on other people's business. He does not say come home. He says that if you asked to be released he would know what to do with you, and that the Secretariat has had its share.

choices.label: Write that the Secretariat has not finished with you
choices.outcome: You write that you are the Holy See's for now, in the careful sentences the service teaches. He writes back a line, in his own hand, that he understands, which is what bishops write when they do not. The chancery finds another man for the vicar's desk, and you read about him in the diocesan paper.

choices.label: Ask the Secretariat to release you to him
choices.outcome: You write to the Secretariat the same week. The answer comes within the month: released, thanked, a medal in a box. {@bishop} meets you at the airport himself, which he has done for no one, and tells you in the car what the desk is.

events.title: Ten Years
events.body: Ten years since the Academy, and the Secretariat's annual letter of leave arrives with a line it did not have before: a priest of the service is reminded of the retreat the Academy makes for its own at the Benedictines above the lake, a week in October, no cipher traffic. You have not made a retreat in six years. There is a report on the elections due the same week.

choices.label: Go up to the lake
choices.outcome: You go up to the lake. The abbot, who was a nuncio once, hears your confession on the fourth day and says nothing about it afterwards except that the service is a hard place to stay a priest and that you are still one. You come down and write the elections report in two days, and it is fine.

choices.label: Write the report; the lake will be there next year
choices.outcome: The report is the best thing you have written: forty pages, read on the Third Loggia, quoted. The lake is there next year, and the year after, and the letter of leave stops mentioning it, and you notice, two Octobers later, that you have stopped noticing.

events.title: Four Hundred Seminarians
events.body: The major seminary has four hundred men, a library with a roof that leaks onto the Fathers, and a rector who asks the nunciature, through you, for money it does not have. The bishops' conference says the seminary is its glory. The rector, when the bishops have gone, says that the glory sleeps three to a room and that half the men should not be there. He wants Rome told. The bishops do not.

choices.label: Tell Rome what the rector said
choices.outcome: You write it plainly: four hundred, three to a room, half of them a mistake, a rector who knows it. The Congregation reads it and asks the conference questions the conference does not enjoy. The rector is moved within the year, and sends you a note that says thank you, without irony, from a parish.

choices.label: Write what the bishops asked
choices.outcome: You write about the glory, and the roof, and the need. Rome sends money for the roof. The rector says nothing to you again. The bishops ask for you at their meetings, which the nuncio notices and uses.

choices.label: Find the roof money from the Americans
choices.outcome: You mention the roof to the ambassador's wife at a dinner and the embassy's small-grants fund fixes it in a season, with a plaque. Rome learns of the plaque before it learns of the roof and is not pleased that a nunciature went to an embassy for a seminary's roof. The rector does not care who paid.

events.title: The Roadblock
events.body: Four hours out on the road to the bishop's funeral, the nunciature's car with its small flag is stopped by six men in parts of uniforms. The driver, who has done this before, reaches under the seat. The Vienna Convention is in your briefcase. The men have a rifle between them and have not eaten today.

choices.label: Let the driver pay
choices.outcome: The driver pays what the driver pays. You arrive at the funeral two hours late and preach, in a borrowed stole, about the Church that keeps going when the state does not. The nuncio, when you tell him, says that the driver has a budget for that and that you should never know what it is.

choices.label: Get out of the car with the flag
choices.outcome: You get out. You say, in their language, who you are and whose car it is, and that the bishop they are burying today was from their district. The oldest of them crosses himself. They let you through and keep the driver's money. The nuncio says you were a fool, and tells the story at every dinner for a year.

events.title: The Patroness's Day
events.body: The feast of the national patroness: a basilica built for ten thousand, the president in the front pew with his generals, the bishops in a row behind him, and the people outside in the square since dawn. The nunciature is placed, by protocol, beside the president. {@nuncio_chief} has a cold, or says he has, and sends you.

choices.label: Sit where the protocol puts you
choices.outcome: You sit beside the president. He talks through the consecration and asks you, during the homily, whether the Holy Father will visit. You say the Holy Father prays for his country every day, which is true of every country. The photograph is in every paper. The bishops see it.

choices.label: Sit with the bishops, and let the president's chair be empty
choices.outcome: You take a chair in the bishops' row and the president's aide spends the Gloria rearranging the protocol. The cardinal archbishop, who has not spoken to a nuncio's secretary in years, asks you to lunch. The ministry of foreign affairs sends a note that is not quite a complaint.

events.title: The Bishop and the Land
events.body: A bishop in the south has said from the pulpit that the land reform is theft and the men behind it are thieves, and named two of them, and one of them is a minister. The ministry asks the nunciature whether the Holy See shares the bishop's view. {@nuncio_chief} asks you to draft the report to Rome and the reply to the ministry, and says that the two should not contradict each other, and that they will.

choices.label: Send the bishop's words to Rome whole, and tell the ministry the Church speaks for the poor
choices.outcome: Rome gets the sermon entire and a note that the bishop is right and imprudent. The ministry gets a sentence it frames. The minister does not receive the nuncio for a year, and the bishop sends the nunciature a case of the south's wine, which the nuncio says you may not drink.

choices.label: Soften the bishop in the report, and the Church in the reply
choices.outcome: Rome reads that a bishop has spoken strongly on a local matter. The ministry reads that the Holy See hopes for justice and dialogue. Nobody is angry. The bishop learns what you wrote and does not write to the nunciature again, and the priests of the south, who hear everything, know your name as the man who softened him.

events.title: The Bureau of Religious Affairs
events.body: The appointment of a bishop here passes, by a sentence in an agreement nobody has read, through the government's Bureau of Religious Affairs, whose director is a courteous man with a file on every priest in the country. He has the Holy See's name for the vacant see and has had it for seven months. He invites you to tea, which is how the bureau says no.

choices.label: Drink the tea, for as long as it takes
choices.outcome: You drink tea with the director every month for a year. He asks about your family and the weather in Rome and never about the name. In the thirteenth month he mentions that the bureau would have no objection to the man, and the man is ordained in the spring. The nuncio says you have learned the one thing the Academy cannot teach.

choices.label: Tell the bishops to pray the name from the pulpit
choices.outcome: You let the bishops know, carefully, that the Holy See has a name and the bureau has not answered. The name is in every church by Sunday. The director stops inviting you to tea. The man is ordained in the autumn, after Rome and the government have had a conversation that does not include you, and the director's file on you is thicker.

events.title: The Village
events.body: A Christian village in the hills has had its church burned, twice, and a catechist beaten, and the police have found nothing to investigate. The bishop asks whether someone from the nunciature could come, not to do anything, but to be seen to have come. It is nine hours by road and the ministry would rather you did not.

choices.label: Go, and be seen
choices.outcome: You go. The catechist meets you at the edge of the village with the whole village behind him, and you say Mass in the burned church with the roof open. The police arrive while you are preaching and stand at the back. The church is not burned a third time. The ministry's note says that the nunciature's travel was not cleared, and the nuncio files it.

choices.label: Send money for the roof, and a letter
choices.outcome: You send what the nunciature can and a letter the bishop reads aloud. The catechist writes to thank you, in careful English, and asks when you will come. You mean to. There is a report due.

events.title: The Eleven O'Clock
events.body: The cathedral's eleven o'clock on an ordinary Sunday: forty people in a nave built for two thousand, a choir of six, a bishop who preaches well to nobody. The Church here is rich from the state's church tax and empty, and the report Rome wants is about the numbers. The bishop would like it to be about the renewal he sees beginning.

choices.label: Write the numbers
choices.outcome: You write the numbers, and the forty, and the choir of six, and the money. Rome reads it in a car and quotes it to the bishop at his next visit, who knows at once whose sentences they are. He is cool at the next three receptions and then, at the fourth, says that it was fair.

choices.label: Write the renewal he sees
choices.outcome: You write about the renewal, which is real and small: a young priest in the suburbs, a Mass for the Poles that is full. Rome reads it and is pleased and learns nothing. The bishop invites you to the renewal, which is twelve people in a hall, and you go, and it is good.

events.title: The Inquiry
events.body: The state's inquiry into the abuse of children in the Church has written to the nunciature asking for its files on three dioceses from the years before the nuncio came. The Holy See's position is that a nunciature is an embassy and its archive inviolable. The victims' lawyers are on the television every night saying so. {@nuncio_chief} has asked Rome and Rome has not answered, and he has asked you what you would do, and he means it.

choices.label: Counsel him to give what the nunciature has
choices.outcome: You tell him that the Convention protects the archive and that the Church cannot be seen to hide behind it on this, of all things. He sends what the nunciature holds, with a note to Rome that he has done it. Rome's answer is silence for a year, and then a transfer for him that is not a promotion. The inquiry says the nunciature cooperated. The bishops say nothing, which is thanks.

choices.label: Counsel him to hold the Convention until Rome speaks
choices.outcome: You tell him the Convention is Rome's to waive and not his. He holds. Rome, when it speaks, speaks of a protocol, and the files are given four years later through the foreign ministry, when nobody is watching. The inquiry's report has a paragraph about the nunciature. You read it twice and put it away.

events.title: The Visa Line
events.body: Every morning there is a line outside the Western embassies, and in it, every morning, there are Christians from the north with a priest's letter saying that they are Christians from the north. They come to the nunciature afterwards, for a second letter, because a letter with the Holy See's seal on it moves a file. The embassies have asked the nunciature, politely, to stop. The patriarch has asked it, less politely, to go on: he is losing his people and would rather lose them alive.

choices.label: Write the letters
choices.outcome: You write the letters, hundreds of them, in the evenings, and sign them with a title you do not have. The embassies complain to Rome through their own channels and Rome asks the nunciature to be prudent, which the nuncio reads aloud and then puts in a drawer. Years later a man in a parish in Michigan shows you the letter, laminated.

choices.label: Stop, as the embassies ask
choices.outcome: You stop. The line still forms, and the nunciature's porter sends it away, and the patriarch does not receive the nuncio for Easter. The embassies are grateful in the way embassies are. You say Mass for the ones who stayed.

events.title: The Patriarch's Anteroom
events.body: The patriarch of the Eastern Church here is older than the nunciature and treats it as a Latin innovation. He receives the nuncio twice a year, for form, and the nuncio's secretary not at all. The nuncio needs something from him that cannot wait for Easter and has sent you with a letter, and the patriarch's deacon has put you in an anteroom with a glass of water and gone away.

choices.label: Wait, all day if need be
choices.outcome: You wait. At four the deacon brings tea. At six the patriarch comes out himself, an old man in black with a staff, and looks at you for some time and says that the Latins have at last sent someone who knows how to sit. He reads the letter standing up and answers it from memory. You are received every month after that, before the nuncio.

choices.label: Leave the letter, and go to the Latin bishop instead
choices.outcome: You leave the letter with the deacon and go to the Latin bishop, who is helpful and has no standing. The patriarch's answer comes at Easter, to the nuncio, and mentions that a young man of the nunciature could not wait an afternoon. The nuncio says nothing, and sends someone else next time.

events.title: The Bishop Who Comes by Boat
events.body: A bishop of the islands has written that he will come to the nunciature for the conference, by boat, in four days, with two priests and a catechist, and that the boat is his cathedral's and leaks. He asks, since the nunciature is on the coast, whether its secretary would like to come back with him for a week and see a diocese with no roads. The nuncio says it is not the sort of thing the service does.

choices.label: Go back with him on the boat
choices.outcome: You go. The diocese is ninety islands, a seminary of eleven, and a bishop who swims to one of his parishes. You confirm two hundred children on a beach with a borrowed mitre on the bishop's instruction and a canon lawyer's doubts. The report you write is read aloud at the Congregation, which has never had one like it.

choices.label: Send the papers he needs, and a good lunch
choices.outcome: You give him lunch and the papers and the nunciature's car to the harbour. He writes afterwards to say the boat made it, and encloses a photograph of a church made of coral. You keep it on the desk through two more countries.

events.title: Another National Day
events.body: The national day, in your fourth country. You know the formula now: the stand, the anthem you learned on the plane, the ambassador of the country that is quarrelling with this one placed next to you so that the Holy See can stand between them. The president's speech is two hours long. The French ambassador, beside you, has a flask.

choices.label: Stand the two hours, as the Holy See's man
choices.outcome: You stand. The president's protocol chief notices that the nunciature did not sit when the others did, and the president notices the protocol chief noticing, and the nunciature is placed better at the next one. The French ambassador says you are a fanatic and offers the flask anyway.

choices.label: Take the flask
choices.outcome: You take the flask, twice. The president's speech is still two hours long. The French ambassador becomes the nunciature's friend for three years, which is worth more than the protocol, and tells you things about the ministry over dinner that the nuncio puts in dispatches without attribution.

events.title: The Correspondent
events.body: A foreign correspondent you knew in the last country has turned up in this one, as they do, and knows that you know things. She is writing about the government's war in the north and the Church's part in it, which is real, and wants the nunciature's view, which she will print as 'a Vatican source'. {@nuncio_chief} has a rule about journalists, and a rule about this one.

choices.label: Have lunch, and say nothing printable
choices.outcome: You have lunch and say nothing she can use and she prints 'a Vatican source' anyway, with a sentence you did not say and would have. The nuncio reads it and asks whether it was you and you say no, which is true, and he believes you, which is the point of three years.

choices.label: Tell her the truth, off the record, and trust her
choices.outcome: You tell her what the nunciature knows about the north, off the record. She keeps it off the record and writes a better piece for it, and the government, which cannot prove anything, lets the nuncio know it suspects. Years later, in Rome, she sends you a book with a dedication that does not name you.

events.title: A Bishop of Your Own Terna
events.body: The first name you sent on a terna has come back from Rome as a bishop, and the bishops' conference asks the nuncio to be the principal consecrator, as nuncios are. He is a quiet man from a mountain diocese who did not expect it and is afraid of it, which is why you put him first. The cathedral holds four thousand and the government has sent a minister, in case.

choices.label: Preach to him about the people
choices.outcome: You preach about his people, whom he knows, and not about Rome, which he does not. He weeps once, at the litany, and is a good bishop for twenty years, and writes to you at Christmas in every country after. The minister leaves before the end.

choices.label: Preach about communion with Rome, for the minister's benefit
choices.outcome: You preach about Peter, and communion, and the Holy Father's care for this country, in sentences the minister can report. The bishop listens carefully and does as he is told for ten years and then, in a crisis, does not. The minister stays to the end and is photographed with you.

events.title: The Bishop of Your Own Diocese
events.body: {@bishop} is in the country on a pilgrimage with forty parishioners and a bus, and comes to the nunciature in a clerical shirt to see the man he ordained, who is now an archbishop and the pope's representative and receives him in a room with a flag. He calls you by your first name in front of the staff, and then corrects himself, and then does it again.

choices.label: Tell him to go on calling you by your first name
choices.outcome: You tell him to go on. He does, through the lunch and the tour of the chapel, and tells the staff stories about your first parish that they repeat for a year. He says, at the car, that the diocese is proud of you and does not know what to do with that, and that he does not either.

choices.label: Let the protocol stand
choices.outcome: You let the protocol stand, gently. He is Excellency and you are Excellency and the lunch is correct. He says at the car that the diocese is proud of you, and you believe him, and you watch the bus go and stand in the courtyard for some time.
